#### Derivation of Equation (6):.

To simplify $\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)$ defined in (5), we note the following

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)~=~ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}b_{k,j}\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)t\right) \displaystyle=~ \displaystyle\frac{b_{k,j}}{n}\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)t\right) \displaystyle=~ \displaystyle\frac{b_{k,j}}{n}\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)\frac{1-\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right)}{1-\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)}. $$

The numerator of the last term in (B-1) can be rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle 1-\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right) \displaystyle=~ \displaystyle\exp\left(\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right)\left(\exp\left(-\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right)-\exp\left(\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right)\right) \displaystyle=~ \displaystyle-2i\exp\left(\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right)\sin\left(\pi\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right). $$

Similarly, the denominator of the last term in (B-1) can be rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle 1-\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)=-2i\exp\left(\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)\sin\left(\pi\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right). $$

Therefore, we obtain Equation (6) by simplifying (B-1)

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)~=~ \displaystyle\frac{b_{k,j}}{n}\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)\frac{\exp\left(\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right)\cdotp\sin\left(\pi\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right)}{\exp\left(\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)\cdotp\sin\left(\pi\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)} \displaystyle~=~ \displaystyle\frac{b_{k,j}}{n}\exp\left(2\pi i\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\frac{n+1}{2}\right)\frac{\sin\left(\pi\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)n\right)}{\sin\left(\pi\left(\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v\right)\right)}, $$

and we can immediately get $\displaystyle{\lim_{n\to\infty}|\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)|=0}$ . ∎

### B.2 Proofs in Section 4.1

The main techniques used in the following proofs are concentration inequalities for random variables. We start with a technical lemma (Theorem 1 in Nagy and Totik (2013)) which will be used in the proof of Lemma 1.

#### Lemma 14.

Suppose $\omega\in(0,\pi]$ and $p_{n}$ is a polynomial of complex number with degree no more than $n$ , then the following holds for all $\theta\in(-\omega,+\omega)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left|p_{n}^{\prime}(e^{i\theta})\right|\leq\frac{n}{2}\left(1+\frac{\sqrt{2}\cos(\theta/2)}{\sqrt{\cos(\theta)-\cos(\omega)}}\right)\sup_{\phi\in[-\omega,\omega]}\left|p_{n}(e^{i\phi})\right|. $$

In particular, when $\omega=\pi$ , then ${\sup_{|z|\leq 1}|p_{n}^{\prime}(z)|\leq n\sup_{|z|\leq 1}|p_{n}(z)|}$ .

#### Proof of Lemma 1:

The DFT of the noise can be expressed as

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t}\exp\left(-2\pi ivt\right)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t}\cos\left(2\pi vt\right)-\frac{i}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t}\sin\left(2\pi vt\right). $$

For any $\delta>0$ , by the union bound, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|>\delta\right) \displaystyle~=~\mathsf{P}\left(|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|^{2}>\delta^{2}\right) \displaystyle~\leq~\mathsf{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t}\cos\left(2\pi vt\right)\right|^{2}>\frac{1}{2}\delta^{2}\right)+\mathsf{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t}\sin\left(2\pi vt\right)\right|^{2}>\frac{1}{2}\delta^{2}\right). $$

We analyze the first term of (B-2) in the following and the second term can be done analogously. For a given $v$ , $\sum_{t=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t}\cos\left(2\pi vt\right)$ is the sum of independent sub-Gaussian random variables with parameter $\sigma^{2}$ , and thus $\sum_{t=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t}\cos\left(2\pi vt\right)$ is a sub-Gaussian random variable with parameter $\sum_{t=1}^{n}\sigma^{2}\cos^{2}\left(2\pi vt\right)$ . Hence, the property of sub-Gaussian random variable in Assumption 2 gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\epsilon_{t}\cos\left(2\pi vt\right)\right|^{2}>\frac{1}{2}\delta^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{n^{2}\delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\cos^{2}\left(2\pi vt\right)}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{n\delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right). $$

By combining the bounds for the two terms in (B-2), for a given $v\in[0,1/2]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|>\delta\right)\leq 4\exp\left(-\frac{n\delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right). $$

Note that $\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)$ can be viewed as an $n$ -degree polynomial of $\exp(-2\pi iv)$ , and let $p_{n}$ denote this polynomial. For any $v_{1},v_{2}\in[0,1/2]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lvert\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{1})-\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{2})\rvert \displaystyle~=~\lvert p_{n}(\exp(-2\pi iv_{1}))-p_{n}(\exp(-2\pi iv_{2}))\rvert \displaystyle~=~\left|\int_{\exp(-2\pi iv_{2})}^{\exp(-2\pi iv_{1})}p^{\prime}_{n}(z)dz\right| \displaystyle~\leq~\lvert\exp\left(-2\pi iv_{1}\right)-\exp(-2\pi iv_{2})\rvert\sup_{\lvert z\rvert\leq 1}\lvert p_{n}^{\prime}(z)\rvert \displaystyle~\leq~\lvert\exp\left(-2\pi iv_{1}\right)-\exp(-2\pi iv_{2})\rvert n\sup_{\lvert z\rvert\leq 1}\lvert p_{n}(z)\rvert, $$

where the last step follows from Lemma 14. The maximum modulus principle of analytic functions implies that $\sup_{\lvert z\rvert\leq 1}\lvert p_{n}(z)\rvert$ must be attained at the boundary $\{z:\lvert z\rvert=1\}$ as $\sup_{\lvert z\rvert\leq 1}\lvert p_{n}(z)\rvert=\sup_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert p_{n}(z)\rvert=\sup_{v\in[0,1]}\lvert\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)\rvert$ . Moreover, since $|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|=|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(1-v)|$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lvert\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{1})-\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{2})\rvert \displaystyle~\leq~\lvert\exp\left(-2\pi iv_{1}\right)-\exp(-2\pi iv_{2})\rvert n\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)| \displaystyle~\leq~2\lvert\sin(\pi(v_{1}-v_{2}))\rvert n\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)| \displaystyle~\leq~2n\pi\lvert v_{1}-v_{2}\rvert\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|. $$

Suppose that we divide the frequency domain $[0,1/2]$ into $L\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ equal intervals, and we let $v_{l}^{\text{mid}}$ denote the middle point of the interval $[\frac{l-1}{2L},\frac{l}{2L}]$ for $l=1,...,L$ . We also suppose that $\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|$ is attained at $v_{\epsilon}^{*}$ which locates in the interval $[\frac{l^{*}-1}{2L},\frac{l^{*}}{2L}]$ , and thus we have $\left|v_{\epsilon}^{*}-v_{l^{*}}^{\text{mid}}\right|<\frac{1}{4L}$ . By applying the inequality (B-4), we find the following

$$ \displaystyle|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{\epsilon}^{*})|-|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{l^{*}}^{\text{mid}})|\leq\left|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{\epsilon}^{*}-v_{l^{*}}^{\text{mid}})\right|\leq\frac{n\pi}{2L}\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)| \displaystyle\implies \displaystyle\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|=|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{\epsilon}^{*})|\leq\max_{l=1,...,L}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{l}^{\text{mid}})|+\frac{n\pi}{2L}\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)| \displaystyle\implies \displaystyle\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|\leq\left(1-\frac{n\pi}{2L}\right)^{-1}\max_{l=1,...,L}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{l}^{\text{mid}})|. $$

Then, we apply the result from (B-3) and the union bound to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|\geq\delta\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathsf{P}\left(\max_{l=1,...,L}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v_{l}^{\text{mid}})|\geq\left(1-\frac{n\pi}{2L}\right)\delta\right) \displaystyle\leq 4L\exp\left(-\frac{n\delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\left(1-\frac{\pi n}{2L}\right)^{2}\right) $$

The lemma is proved by choosing $L=12n$ as following

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|\geq\delta\right)~\leq~48n\exp\left(-\frac{n\delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\left(1-\frac{\pi}{24}\right)^{2}\right). $$

Specifically, if we choose the upper bound $\delta$ as $\bar{\epsilon}_{v}=\frac{2\sigma H}{1-\pi/24}\sqrt{\frac{\log(n)}{n}}$ defined in Step 10 of Algorithm 1, then we have ${\mathsf{P}\bigg(\sup_{v\in[0,1/2]}|\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}(v)|\geq\bar{\epsilon}_{v}\bigg)\leq\frac{48}{n^{H^{2}-1}}}$ . ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 2:

Recall that we defined $\mathcal{V}_{k}=[0,1/2]\cap\{\cup_{j:|b_{k,j}|>0}[\frac{j}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n}]\}$ and $\overline{\mathcal{V}}_{k}=[0,1/2]\setminus\mathcal{V}_{k}$ , where $\mathcal{V}_{k}$ represents the union of neighborhoods of all present frequencies. To prove Lemma 2, it is more natural to start from investigating the leakage in sets $\mathcal{U}_{k}\coloneqq[0,1/2]\cap\{\cup_{j:}[\frac{j}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n}]\}$ and $\overline{\mathcal{U}}_{k}=[0,1/2]\setminus\mathcal{U}_{k}$ . Note that $\mathcal{U}_{k}$ differs from $\mathcal{V}_{k}$ by removing the requirement $|b_{k,j}|>0$ , so $\mathcal{U}_{k}$ represents the union of neighborhoods around all possible locations of present frequencies and $\mathcal{V}_{k}$ is a subset of $\mathcal{U}_{k}$ , i.e., $\mathcal{V}_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{k}$ .

Given the expression of $\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)$ in (6) and the definition of $B_{k}$ in (11), we can show

$$ \displaystyle\lvert\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)\rvert\leq|b_{k,j}|\left|\frac{\sin\left(\pi(j/T_{k}-v)n\right)}{n\sin\left(\pi(j/T_{k}-v)\right)}\right|\leq B_{k}\left|\frac{\sin\left(\pi(j/T_{k}-v)n\right)}{n\sin\left(\pi(j/T_{k}-v)\right)}\right|. $$

Define a function $\displaystyle{R(\theta)\coloneqq\left|\frac{\sin\left(\pi n\theta\right)}{n\sin\left(\pi\theta\right)}\right|}$ and then we have (B-7). Note that $R(\theta)$ will play a critical role in this proof.

$$ |\tilde{\mu}_{k}(v)|\leq\sum_{j=0}^{T_{k}-1}|\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)|\leq B_{k}\sum_{j=0}^{T_{k}-1}R(j/T_{k}-v). $$

We first examine the leakage for $v\in\bar{}\mathcal{U}_{k}$ . Suppose that $v\in[\frac{j^{\prime}}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j^{\prime}+1}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}]$ for some $j^{\prime}\in\left\{0,\dots,\lfloor\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\rfloor\right\}$ . We decompose the sum $\sum_{j=0}^{T_{k}-1}R(j/T_{k}-v)$ in (B-7) into three terms as following, and we bound each term using properties $R(\theta)=R(-\theta)$ and $R(\theta)=R(1-\theta)$ .

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{j^{\prime}}R(j/T_{k}-v)=\sum_{j=0}^{j^{\prime}}R(v-j/T_{k})\leq\sum_{j=0}^{j^{\prime}}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j+1}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}\right]\right\}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=j^{\prime}+1}^{j^{\prime}+\lfloor\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\rfloor+1}R(j/T_{k}-v)\leq\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\rfloor}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j+1}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}\right]\right\}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=j^{\prime}+\lfloor\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\rfloor+2}^{T_{k}-1}R(j/T_{k}-v) \displaystyle~\leq~\sum_{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\rfloor+1}^{T_{k}-j^{\prime}-2}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j+1}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}\right]\right\} \displaystyle~=~\sum_{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\rfloor+1}^{T_{k}-j^{\prime}-2}\sup\left\{R(1-\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j+1}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}\right]\right\} \displaystyle~=~\sum_{j=j^{\prime}+1}^{T_{k}-\lfloor\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\rfloor-2}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j+1}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}\right]\right\}. $$

Combining (B-8), (B-9) and (B-10) together, we can further develop (B-7) as

$$ \displaystyle|\tilde{\mu}_{k}(v)|\leq B_{k}\sum_{j=0}^{T_{k}-1}R(j/T_{k}-v)\leq 2B_{k}\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\rfloor}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j+1}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}\right]\right\}. $$

To analyze the expression (B-11), we need to examine $R(\theta)$ closely. Note that $R(\theta)$ is bounded. Furthermore, the numerator $|\sin\left(\pi n\theta\right)|$ has a period $\frac{1}{n}$ , and the denominator $|n\sin(\pi\theta)|$ is monotonically increasing for $\theta\in[0,1/2]$ . Therefore, we can make the following two remarks. (i) Given $0\leq\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}$ and $\theta_{2}+\frac{1}{n}\leq\frac{1}{2}$ , then $\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in[\theta_{1},\theta_{1}+\frac{1}{n}]\right\}>\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in[\theta_{2},\theta_{2}+\frac{1}{n}]\right\}$ , i.e, for two intervals of the same width $\frac{1}{n}$ in the domain $[0,1/2]$ , the maximum of $R(\theta)$ in the left interval is larger than that in the right interval. (ii) Given $0\leq\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}$ , then $\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in[\theta_{1},\theta_{1}+\frac{1}{n}]\right\}\geq\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in[\theta_{1},\theta_{2}]\right\}$ . We continue the analysis by applying these two properties of $R(\theta)$ .

When $T_{k}$ is even, for $j=0,...,\frac{T_{k}}{2}-1$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j+1}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}\right]\right\}&~\leq~\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g+1}{n}\right]\right\}\\
&~\leq~\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{(2j+1)g}{n},\frac{(2j+1)g+1}{n}\right]\right\}\end{split} $$

where the second step follows from that $\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n}\geq\frac{(2j+1)g}{n}$ since $T_{k}<\frac{n}{2g}$ given by Assumption 3. We also have $\frac{T_{k}}{2}-1\leq\lfloor\frac{n-1}{4g}-1\rfloor=\lfloor\frac{n-4g-1}{4g}\rfloor$ .

When $T_{k}$ is odd, inequality (B-12) holds directly for $j=0,...,\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}-1$ . For $j=\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}$ , although the corresponding interval $\left[\frac{T_{k}-1}{2T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n},\frac{T_{k}+1}{2T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n}\right]$ is not fully contained in $[0,1/2]$ , inequality (B-12) still holds since $R(\theta)$ is symmetric around $\theta=1/2$ . We also have $\frac{T_{k}-1}{2}\leq\lfloor\frac{1}{2}\big(\frac{n-1}{2g}-1\big)\rfloor=\lfloor\frac{n-2g-1}{4g}\rfloor$ .

Combing these two cases, we can further derive (B-11) as

$$ \displaystyle|\tilde{\mu}_{k}(v)|\leq 2B_{k}\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor\frac{(n-2g-1)}{4g}\rfloor}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{(2j+1)g}{n},\frac{(2j+1)g+1}{n}\right]\right\}. $$

Recall that we defined ${A_{j}=\sup\left\{\frac{|\sin(\pi\nu)|}{\pi\nu}:\nu\in[j,j+1]\right\}}$ and ${U_{1}=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor{\frac{n-2g-1}{4g}\rfloor}}A_{(2j+1)g}}$ , and note the fact that $\sin(x)\geq 2x/\pi$ for $x\in[0,\pi/2]$ . Then, we can bound the leakage for $v\in\bar{}\mathcal{U}_{k}$ as

$$ \displaystyle|\tilde{\mu}_{k}(v)| \displaystyle\leq\pi B_{k}\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor\frac{(n-2g-1)}{4g}\rfloor}\sup\left\{\frac{|\sin(\pi n\theta)|}{\pi n\theta}:\theta\in\left[\frac{(2j+1)g}{n},\frac{(2j+1)g+1}{n}\right]\right\} \displaystyle=\pi B_{k}\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor{\frac{n-2g-1}{4g}\rfloor}}A_{(2j+1)g}=\pi B_{k}U_{1}. $$

The analysis of the leakage in $\mathcal{U}_{k}$ can be conducted in an analogous way as above. In addition to further exploiting the properties of $R(\theta)$ , we also utilizing the symmetry of the neighborhood to achieve a finer result. Suppose that $v\in[\frac{j^{\prime}}{T_{k}}-\frac{g}{n},\frac{j^{\prime}}{T_{k}}+\frac{g}{n}]$ for some $j^{\prime}\in\left\{0,\dots,\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor\right\}$ . Let $v^{\prime}=v-\frac{j^{\prime}}{T_{k}}$ and then $v^{\prime}\in[-\frac{g}{n},\frac{g}{n}]$ . We also assume that $v^{\prime}$ falls in the interval $[\frac{j_{0}}{n},\frac{j_{0}+1}{n}]$ for some $j_{0}\in\{-g,...,g-1\}$ . The leakage in the neighborhood of $j^{\prime}/T_{k}$ is contributed by frequency components $j/T_{k}$ with $j\neq j^{\prime}$ . Hence, we decompose $\sum_{j\neq j^{\prime}}R(j/T_{k}-v)$ into three terms as following,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{j^{\prime}-1}R(j/T_{k}-v)=\sum_{j=0}^{j^{\prime}-1}R(v-j/T_{k})\leq\sum_{j=1}^{j^{\prime}}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{j_{0}}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{j_{0}+1}{n}\right]\right\}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=j^{\prime}+1}^{j^{\prime}+\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor}R(j/T_{k}-v)~\leq~ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}-\frac{j_{0}+1}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}-\frac{j_{0}}{n}\right]\right\} \displaystyle~\leq~ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{2jg-j_{0}-1}{n},\frac{2jg-j_{0}}{n}\right]\right\}\leq\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n-1}{4g}\rfloor}A_{2jg-j_{0}-1}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=j^{\prime}+\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor+1}^{T_{k}-1}R(j/T_{k}-v) \displaystyle~\leq~\sum_{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor+1}^{T_{k}-j^{\prime}-1}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}-\frac{j_{0}+1}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}-\frac{j_{0}}{n}\right]\right\} \displaystyle~=~\sum_{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor+1}^{T_{k}-j^{\prime}-1}\sup\left\{R(1-\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}-\frac{j_{0}+1}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}-\frac{j_{0}}{n}\right]\right\} \displaystyle~=~\sum_{j=j^{\prime}+1}^{T_{k}-\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor-1}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{j_{0}}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{j_{0}+1}{n}\right]\right\}. $$

Combining (B-13) and (B-15) together, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{j^{\prime}-1}R(j/T_{k}-v)+\sum_{j=j^{\prime}+\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor+1}^{T_{k}-1}R(j/T_{k}-v) \displaystyle~\leq~ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{j_{0}}{n},\frac{j}{T_{k}}+\frac{j_{0}+1}{n}\right]\right\} \displaystyle~\leq~ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{T_{k}}{2}\rfloor}\sup\left\{R(\theta):\theta\in\left[\frac{2jg+j_{0}}{n},\frac{2jg+j_{0}+1}{n}\right]\right\}\leq\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n-1}{4g}\rfloor}A_{2jg+j_{0}}. $$

Note that $A_{j}$ is monotonically decreasing in $j$ such that $\frac{1}{(j+\frac{1}{2})\pi}\leq A_{j}\leq\frac{1}{j\pi}$ . Moreover, $A_{j-1}+A_{j+1}\geq 2A_{j}$ for all $j\geq 2$ . Recall that we defined ${U_{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor{\frac{n-1}{4g}\rfloor}}A_{2jg-1}}$ . We merge (B-14) and (B-16) together, apply the monotonicity and the convexity of $A_{j}$ , and then we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq j^{\prime}}R(j/T_{k}-v)\leq\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n-1}{4g}\rfloor}A_{2jg-j_{0}-1}+\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n-1}{4g}\rfloor}A_{2jg+j_{0}}\leq\pi\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n-1}{4g}\rfloor}A_{2jg-1}=\pi U_{2}, $$

which leads to $|\sum_{j\not=j^{\prime}}\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)|\leq\sum_{j\not=j^{\prime}}|\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)|\leq B_{k}\sum_{j\neq j^{\prime}}R(v-j/T_{k})\leq\pi B_{k}U_{2}$ .

We show that $U_{1}\geq U_{2}$ by revisiting their definitions as following

$$ \displaystyle U_{1} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor{\frac{n-2g-1}{4g}\rfloor}}A_{(2j+1)g}\geq\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor{\frac{n-4g-1}{4g}\rfloor}}A_{(2j+1)g}=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor{\frac{n-1}{4g}\rfloor}}A_{(2j-1)g}\geq\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor{\frac{n-1}{4g}\rfloor}}A_{2jg-1}=U_{2}. $$

The last inequality is due to $(2j-1)g<2jg-1$ given $g\geq 2$ in Assumption 3.

So far, we have proven

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{v\in\bar{}\mathcal{U}_{k}}\left|\sum_{j=0}^{T_{k}-1}\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)\right|\leq\pi B_{k}U_{1}\text{ and }\sup_{v\in{\mathcal{U}}_{k}}\left|\sum_{j:|\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v|\geq\frac{g}{n}}\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)\right|\leq\pi B_{k}U_{2}\leq\pi B_{k}U_{1}. $$

Since $\mathcal{V}_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{k}$ , we immediately have $\sup_{v\in{\mathcal{V}}_{k}}\left|\sum_{j:|\frac{j}{T_{k}}-v|\geq\frac{g(n)}{n}}\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}(v)\right|\leq\pi B_{k}U_{2}$ . Given Assumption 2 - 4, by applying union bound we have Lemma 4, Lemma 5 and Lemma 7 hold together with probability no less than $1-\frac{48}{n^{H^{2}-1}}-\frac{200}{n^{0.867H^{2}-1}}-\frac{200}{n^{0.694H^{2}-1}}$ . Therefore, the period $T_{k}$ can be correctly estimated accordingly. Theorem 2 implies immediately by applying the above result of a single arm with union bound for $K$ arms.

We also remark on the values of parameters $n$ , $g$ and $H$ used in Algorithm 1. Choosing a large sample size $n$ obviously benefits the period estimation in stage one, but it leaves less time for stage two to exploit rewards. Parameter $g$ is used in determining $U_{1}$ , $U_{2}$ and the width of the neighborhood. A large $g$ relaxes the sample size requirement for condition (14), but it limits the ability to estimate a long period as $T_{k}<\frac{n}{2g}$ is assumed in Assumption 3. Parameter $H$ is used in setting $\bar{\epsilon}_{v}$ and thus is also related to condition (14). A smaller $H$ makes (14) easier to satisfy, but it lowers the probability that all periods are correctly estimated. By considering these trade-offs as a whole, we carefully derive a set of values in (7) which can significantly ease the restriction in (14), and we also note that Algorithm 1 performs well empirically with this setting. ∎

#### Lemma 15.

Suppose that $\{X_{t}:t\in\mathbb{N}^{+}\}$ are independent sub-Gaussian random variables with parameter $\sigma$ . Let $q_{t}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=1}^{t}X_{j}$ . For any $\delta_{0}\in(0,1)$ , then $\mathsf{P}\left(\exists\,t\geq 1,\lvert q_{t}\rvert\geq\sqrt{\frac{4\sigma^{2}}{t}\log\left(\frac{4t}{\delta_{0}}\right)}\right)\leq\delta_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

Define $Q_{n}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}$ . Since $Q_{n}$ is the sum of independent sub-Gaussian random variables, $Q_{n}$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter $\sqrt{n}\sigma$ , and $\mathsf{E}[\exp(\lambda Q_{n})]\leq\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}n\sigma^{2}\lambda^{2}\right)$ holds for all $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ according to the sub-Gaussian property described in Assumption 2. For any $\eta>0$ , we have the following by choosing $\lambda=\frac{\eta}{n\sigma^{2}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(\exists t\leq n,Q_{t}\geq\eta\right) \displaystyle=\mathsf{P}\left(\max_{t\leq n}\exp(\lambda Q_{t})\geq\exp(\lambda\eta)\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{\mathsf{E}\left[\exp(\lambda Q_{n})\right]}{\exp(\lambda\eta)}\leq\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}n\sigma^{2}\lambda^{2}-\lambda\eta\right)=\exp\left(-\frac{\eta^{2}}{2n\sigma^{2}}\right). $$

The first inequality holds from Doob’s submartingale inequality and the fact that $Q_{t}$ is a submartingale with respect to the filtration generated by $X_{1},...,X_{n}$ .

By symmetry, we also have $\mathsf{P}\left(\exists t\leq n,Q_{t}\leq-\eta\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\eta^{2}}{2n\sigma^{2}}\right)$ , and therefore

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(\exists t\leq n,\lvert Q_{t}\rvert\geq\eta\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\eta^{2}}{2n\sigma^{2}}\right). $$

Then, we can show

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(\exists\,t\geq 1,\lvert Q_{t}\rvert\geq\sqrt{4\sigma^{2}t\log\left(\frac{4t}{\delta_{0}}\right)}\right) \displaystyle\leq~ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\mathsf{P}\left(2^{j}\leq t<2^{j+1},\lvert Q_{t}\rvert\geq\sqrt{4\sigma^{2}t\log\left(\frac{4t}{\delta_{0}}\right)}\right) \displaystyle\leq~ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\mathsf{P}\left(1\leq t\leq 2^{j+1},\lvert Q_{t}\rvert\geq\sqrt{4\sigma^{2}\cdot 2^{j}\cdot\log\left(\frac{4\cdot 2^{j}}{\delta_{0}}\right)}\right) \displaystyle\leq~ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}2\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\cdot 2^{j+1}\sigma^{2}}\cdot 4\sigma^{2}\cdot 2^{j}\cdot\log\left(\frac{4\cdot 2^{j}}{\delta_{0}}\right)\right)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{\delta_{0}}{2^{j+1}}=\delta_{0}, $$

where the first inequality follows the union bound and the last inequality applies the knowledge of (B-27). The lemma follows immediately by dividing $Q_{t}$ by $t$ . ∎

### B.4 Proofs in Section 5

The following proofs provide the regret lower bounds for three classes of bandits, namely $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ , $\mathcal{E}_{2}(T_{1})$ and $\mathcal{E}_{3}(T_{1},...,T_{K})$ , discussed in Section 5. In particular, $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ is defined as the class of $K$ -armed unit-variance Gaussian bandits where all arms are stationary, $\mathcal{E}_{2}(T_{1})$ is similar to $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ except that its first arm has a (minimum) period $T_{1}$ , and $\mathcal{E}_{3}(T_{1},...,T_{K})$ is the class where all arms are periodic with (minimum) periods $T_{1},...,T_{K}$ . By these definitions, bandits in these classes satisfy Assumption 1 and 2, and we assume the periods of arms satisfy Assumption 3 as well. For simplicity, we abbreviate $\mathcal{E}_{2}(T_{1})$ as $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{3}(T_{1},...,T_{K})$ as $\mathcal{E}_{3}$ when it does not effect reading.

#### Proof of Lemma 12:.

This Lemma is an easy implication of the regret lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{TK})$ of the classic stationary MAB problem. For completeness, we provide an independent proof here. The techniques can be referred to Chapter 15 of Lattimore and Szepesvári (2020) (hereafter LS2020).

We first study a simple case where $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ is the class of two-armed bandits. Let $\Delta\in(0,0.5)$ be a parameter to be chosen later. Consider two instances $\nu_{1}$ and $\nu_{2}$ in $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ , specifically $\nu_{1}$ with mean rewards $\{\mu_{1}^{(\nu_{1})}=0.5+\Delta,~\mu_{2}^{(\nu_{1})}=0.5\}$ and $\nu_{2}$ with mean rewards $\{\mu_{1}^{(\nu_{2})}=0.5-\Delta,~\mu_{2}^{(\nu_{2})}=0.5\}$ , where the superscript on $\mu$ denotes the MAB instance to which the arm belongs.

Let $C_{1}(T)$ count the number of epochs when the first arm is pulled during the horizon $T$ , and $C_{2}(T)$ count that of the second arm. For an arbitrary policy $\pi$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{E}_{\nu_{1}}[R^{\pi}_{T}]\geq\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{1}}\left(C_{1}(T)\leq T/2\right)\frac{T\Delta}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathsf{E}_{\nu_{2}}[R^{\pi}_{T}]\geq\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{2}}\left(C_{1}(T)>T/2\right)\frac{T\Delta}{2}. $$

Since $2\max\{a,b\}\geq a+b$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{E}_{1}}\mathsf{E}_{\nu}[R_{T}^{\pi}]\geq\frac{1}{2}\big(\mathsf{E}_{\nu_{1}}[R^{\pi}_{T}]+\mathsf{E}_{\nu_{2}}[R^{\pi}_{T}]\big)\geq\big(\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{1}}\left(C_{1}(T)\leq T/2\right)+\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{2}}\left(C_{1}(T)>T/2\right)\big)\frac{T\Delta}{4}. $$

Then we apply the Bretagnolle-Huber inequality (Theorem 14.2 in LS2020) and get

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{E}_{1}}\mathsf{E}_{\nu}[R_{T}^{\pi}]\geq\exp\left(-D(\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{1}},\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{2}})\right)\frac{T\Delta}{8}, $$

where $D(\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{1}},\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{2}})$ is the Kullback-Leibler divergence (also known as the relative entropy) from $\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{1}}$ to $\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{2}}$ . We can further simplify $D(\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{1}},\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{2}})$ using Lemma 15.1 in LS2020 to obtain

$$ \displaystyle D(\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{1}},\mathsf{P}_{\nu_{2}})= \displaystyle\mathsf{E}_{\nu_{1}}\left[C_{1}(T)\right]D\left(\mathcal{N}(0.5+\Delta,1),\mathcal{N}(0.5-\Delta,1)\right)+\mathsf{E}_{\nu_{1}}\left[C_{2}(T)\right]D\left(\mathcal{N}(0.5,1),\mathcal{N}(0.5,1)\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\mathsf{E}_{\nu_{1}}\left[C_{1}(T)\right]\Delta^{2}\leq 2T\Delta^{2}. $$

If we set $\Delta=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2T}}$ , then we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{E}_{1}}\mathsf{E}_{\nu}[R_{T}^{\pi}]\geq\exp\left(-2T\Delta^{2}\right)\frac{T\Delta}{8}=\frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}e}\sqrt{T}. $$

For $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ with bandits of $K>2$ arms, since $\mu_{2},...,\mu_{K}$ are already known, we can always choose the best arm among $K\geq 2$ and discard the suboptimal ones at the beginning of the decision horizon, i.e., it actually reduces to the case of $K=2$ . Hence, the lower bound in (B-45) applies and this proves the result. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 13:.

By keeping the best arm and discarding suboptimal ones among arms $k\geq 2$ , we only need to consider a reduced case of $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ with two arms.

Given $T_{1}$ is known, we can treat the decision scenarios at the same phase of each cycle as an independent stationary MAB, and hence each instance in $\mathcal{E}_{2}(T_{1})$ can be decomposed into $T_{1}$ independent sub-instances, each of which belongs to $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ and takes a decision horizon at least of $\lfloor T/T_{1}\rfloor$ . Applying Lemma 12, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{E}_{2}}\mathsf{E}_{\nu}[R_{T}^{\pi}]\geq T_{1}\sup_{\nu^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}_{1}}\mathsf{E}_{\nu^{\prime}}[R_{\lfloor T/T_{1}\rfloor}^{\pi}]\geq\frac{T_{1}}{8\sqrt{2}e}\sqrt{\lfloor T/T_{1}\rfloor}\geq\frac{1}{16e}\sqrt{TT_{1}}. $$

The last inequality holds since Assumption 3 implies $\lfloor\frac{T}{T_{1}}\rfloor\geq\frac{T}{\sqrt{2}T_{1}}$ . This completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3:.

Since all arms are symmetric, we only need to prove

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal{E}_{3}}\mathsf{E}_{\nu}[R_{T}^{\pi}]\geq\frac{1}{32e}\sqrt{TT_{1}}. $$

When $T_{2}=...=T_{K}=1$ , $\mathcal{E}_{3}(T_{1},...,T_{K})$ degenerates to $\mathcal{E}_{2}(T_{1})$ , and hence we can invoke Lemma 13 to obtain (B-47). However, if we consider $\mathcal{E}_{3}$ with $T_{k}\geq 2$ for some $k\geq 2$ , i.e., certain arms are indeed non-stationary, the above argument does not proceed. Note that the expected regret $f_{\pi}(\nu)\coloneqq\mathsf{E}_{\nu}[R_{T}^{\pi}]$ can be viewed as a functional of $\nu\in\mathcal{E}_{2}\cup\mathcal{E}_{3}$ with parameter $\pi$ . To establish a general lower bound, we introduce a metric for any pair of MAB instances $(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})$ in $\mathcal{E}_{2}\cup\mathcal{E}_{3}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{p=1}^{T_{k}}\left(\mu_{k,p}^{(\nu_{1})}-\mu_{k,p}^{(\nu_{2})}\right)^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

We have the following two facts with the metric $\mathcal{M}$ :

- 1. $\mathcal{E}_{3}$ is dense in $\mathcal{E}_{2}\cup\mathcal{E}_{3}$ . For any instance $\nu_{1}\in\mathcal{E}_{2}(T_{1})$ , by perturbing its mean rewards $\mu_{k,t}^{(\nu_{1})}$ for certain arms $k\geq 2$ , we can make these arms periodic and hence obtain a new instance $\nu_{2}\in\mathcal{E}_{3}(T_{1},...,T_{K})$ which has the required periods. For any $\delta>0$ , we can make such perturbation slight enough to achieve $\mathcal{M}(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})<\delta$ .

- 2. $f_{\pi}(\nu)$ is continuous in $\nu$ and this continuity is uniform with respect to $\pi$ . Specifically, given $\nu_{1}\in\mathcal{E}_{2}\cup\mathcal{E}_{3}$ , for any $\epsilon>0$ , there exists $\delta>0$ such that $\lvert f_{\pi}(\nu_{1})-f_{\pi}(\nu_{2})\rvert<\epsilon$ holds for any $\nu_{2}\in\mathcal{E}_{2}\cup\mathcal{E}_{3}$ with $\mathcal{M}(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})<\delta$ .

For any policy $\pi$ that knows $T_{k}$ ’s, Lemma 13 implies that some $\nu_{1}\in\mathcal{E}_{2}$ yields $f_{\pi}(\nu_{1})\geq\frac{1}{16e}\sqrt{TT_{1}}$ . As a result of above two facts, when choosing $\epsilon=\frac{1}{32e}\sqrt{TT_{1}}$ and slightly perturbing $\nu_{1}$ accordingly, we can always find a suitable $\nu_{2}\in\mathcal{E}_{3}$ satisfying $\lvert f_{\pi}(\nu_{1})-f_{\pi}(\nu_{2})\rvert<\epsilon$ . Therefore, we have

$$ \displaystyle f_{\pi}(\nu_{2})\geq f_{\pi}(\nu_{1})-\lvert f_{\pi}(\nu_{1})-f_{\pi}(\nu_{2})\rvert\geq\frac{1}{32e}\sqrt{TT_{1}}, $$

which leads to Theorem 3.

The first fact is quite obvious. For example, given a set of periods $\{T_{1},...,T_{K}\}$ and any $\nu_{1}\in\mathcal{E}_{2}(T_{1})$ , we may create $\nu_{2}$ by setting its mean rewards as the following perturbation,

$$ \mu_{k,t}^{(\nu_{2})}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\mu_{k,t}^{(\nu_{1})}+\delta/\sqrt{2K},&\quad\text{for any arm $k\geq 2$ with $T_{k}\geq 2$ and any $t\equiv 1(\mathrm{mod}\,T_{k})$},\\
\mu_{k,t}^{(\nu_{1})},&\quad\text{otherwise}.\\
\end{array}\right. $$

Therefore, $\nu_{2}$ has the required periods, i.e., $\nu_{2}\in\mathcal{E}_{3}(T_{1},...,T_{K})$ , and satisfies $\mathcal{M}(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})<\delta$ .

Next we prove the second fact. Given a bandit instance, we denote the random actions and rewards generated by a policy $\pi$ as $(\pi_{1},Y_{\pi_{1},1},\dots,\pi_{T},Y_{\pi_{T},T})$ , and we denote the realized actions and rewards as $(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{T},y_{T})$ . The pseudo-regret can be expressed as $R_{T}^{\pi}(\pi_{1},Y_{\pi_{1},1},\dots,\pi_{T},Y_{\pi_{T},T})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Delta_{a_{t},t}$ , where $\Delta_{a_{t},t}\leq 1$ is the gap between the optimal mean reward and the mean reward of arm $a_{t}$ pulled at epoch $t$ . We integrate $R_{T}^{\pi}$ over the distribution of $(\pi_{1},Y_{\pi_{1},1},\dots,\pi_{T},Y_{\pi_{T},T})$ , which can be represented by

$$ \displaystyle q(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{T},y_{T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi(a_{t}|a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},y_{t-1})p(y_{t}-\mu_{a_{t},t}), $$

where $p(\cdot)$ is the PDF of the standard normal distribution. Then we have

$$ \displaystyle f_{\pi}(\nu)= \displaystyle~\int R_{T}^{\pi}(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{T},y_{T})q(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{T},y_{T})d\psi(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{T},y_{T}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle~\int\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Delta_{a_{t},t}\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi(a_{t}|a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},y_{t-1})p(y_{t}-\mu_{a_{t},t})\mathrm{d}\psi(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{T},y_{T}), $$

where $\psi$ is the product of the counting measures and Lebesgue measures on $(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{T},y_{T})$ .

For two instances $\nu_{1}$ and $\nu_{2}$ in $\mathcal{E}_{2}\cup\mathcal{E}_{3}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lvert f_{\pi}(\nu_{1})-f_{\pi}(\nu_{2})\rvert\leq T\int\left|\prod_{t=1}^{T}p\left(y_{t}-\mu^{(\nu_{1})}_{a_{t},t}\right)-\prod_{t=1}^{T}p\left(y_{t}-\mu^{(\nu_{2})}_{a_{t},t}\right)\right|\mathrm{d}\psi. $$

We then invoke Lebesgue’s dominated convergence theorem. For fixed $(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{T},y_{T})$ , when $\mathcal{M}(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})\to 0$ , we must have

$$ \left|\prod_{t=1}^{T}p\left(y_{t}-\mu^{(\nu_{1})}_{a_{t},t}\right)-\prod_{t=1}^{T}p\left(y_{t}-\mu^{(\nu_{2})}_{a_{t},t}\right)\right|\to 0. $$

Moreover, it is easy to see that it is dominated by an integrable function because of the light tail of Gaussian distributions and the fact that $\mu_{a_{t},t}^{(\nu_{1})},\mu_{a_{t},t}^{(\nu_{2})}\in[0,1]$ . As a result, $\lvert f_{\pi}(\nu_{1})-f_{\pi}(\nu_{2})\rvert\to 0$ and the convergence is uniform with respect to $\pi$ . This proves the second fact. ∎

## Appendix C Periodic MAB with the Same Period

In the main text of this paper, we consider a very general periodic MAB model where we do not impose any assumption on the length of period or the structure of variation for the mean reward of any arm. We develop a two-stage policy with a regret upper bound $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T\sum_{k=1}^{K}T_{k}})$ and we show a general lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{T\max_{k}\{T_{k}\}})$ for any policy. In practice, the DM may face special (or simplified) settings where the periodic evolution of mean rewards enjoy certain possess. For example, all arms may have the same period. It is a common case that the demands of various products tend to have the same seasonal pattern in the learning and earning problem of dynamic pricing. Regardless of the pricing policy, the seasonality of the demand, in particular, its period, is typically exogenous and largely unaltered.

In this appendix, we investigate a specific setting of the periodic MAB model where the mean rewards of all arms vary over time with the same period, i.e., $T_{1}=...=T_{K}$ . We assume that Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 still hold. Comparing to Algorithm 2 designed for the general periodic MAB problem, it is possible to develop more efficient learning algorithms with smaller regret upper bound by exploiting the property of the same period, and it is also possible to establish a matching regret lower bound. We may still use Algorithm 1 to estimate the (common) length of periods. Recall that it incurs a regret of $O(\sqrt{TK})$ in stage one and the regret caused by the wrong estimation is negligible in stage two. Because estimating periods does not incur significant regret, to simplify the discussion, we may assume $T_{k}$ ’s are known in advance and focus on the learning of rewards.

### C.1 Same Period without Other Structures

When $T_{1}=...=T_{K}$ , the learning problem can be decomposed into $T_{1}$ subproblems, each of which is a classic stationary MAB problem with $K$ arms and learning horizon $T/T_{1}$ . Without additional seasonality structures, these subproblems are independent of each other, and hence need to be learned separately. As a result, the optimal rate of regret $O(T_{1}\sqrt{KT/T_{1}})=O(\sqrt{KTT_{1}})$ can be achieved when applying classic MAB algorithms, e.g., UCB, to each subproblem. Note that in this case, the regret bound in Theorem 1 matches the lower bound.

### C.2 Same Period with a Fixed Best Arm

In addition to sharing a common period, suppose that the best arm remains as the same over time. More precisely, there exists $k\in\mathcal{K}$ such that $\mu_{k,t}=\max_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}}\mu_{k^{\prime},t}$ for all $t=1,\dots,T_{1}$ . This is a frequently encountered situation in practice, for example, arms (selling of products) have the same seasonality and their mean rewards (demands) evolve in parallel. Given the knowledge that the best arm is fixed, we propose the following sequential-elimination-based learning policy.

*Algorithm 3 sequential-elimination-based learning*

```
1: Input: $T$ , $K$ , $\sigma$ and $T_{1}$
2: Initialize $\mathcal{A}_{1}\leftarrow\left\{1,\dots,K\right\}$
3: for $s=1,2,...$ do
4: Choose $n_{s}=\lceil 2^{2+2s}\log(KTs^{2})/T_{1}\rceil T_{1}$
5: Pull each arm $k\in\mathcal{A}_{s}$ exactly $n_{s}$ times and let $m_{k}^{(s)}$ be the average of these rewards
6: Update active set $\mathcal{A}_{s+1}\leftarrow\left\{k\in\mathcal{A}_{s}:m_{k}^{(s)}\geq\max_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{s}}m_{k^{\prime}}^{(s)}-2^{-s}\sigma\right\}$
7: end for
```

Comparing to Algorithm 2, Algorithm 3 relies on the similar idea of gradually eliminating clearly suboptimal arms. However, the implementation is simpler. Since one arm always has the highest mean reward at each phase of the common period, we pool the information together to infer the optimal arm instead of tracking each individual phase separately. Specifically, the number of each arm pulled in round $s$ , i.e., $n_{s}$ chosen in Step 4, is a multiple of $T_{1}$ , hence the estimator $m_{k}^{(s)}$ is for the average of mean rewards $\sum_{t=1}^{T_{1}}\mu_{k,t}/T_{1}$ in a period. In the following, we show that Algorithm 3 achieves a regret upper bound $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{TK})$ , which matches the regret lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{TK})$ for any policy in this setting.

#### Proof.

The regret lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{TK})$ is provided by the result of the classic stationary MAB model as it is a special case here. For the regret upper bound, Algorithm 3 is extended from Exercise 6.8 in LS2020 which applies to the classic stationary MAB problem, and our regret analysis tackles the difficulty introduced by the periodic mean rewards.

Without loss of generality, we assume that arm 1 is the best arm. Let $\bar{\mu}_{k}:=\frac{1}{T_{1}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{1}}\mu_{k,t}$ denote the average of mean rewards in a period for arm $k\in\mathcal{K}$ . Let $\bar{\Delta}_{k}:=\bar{\mu}_{1}-\bar{\mu}_{k}$ denote the average suboptimal gap of arm $k$ . Given $\mu_{k,t}\in[0,1]$ imposed by Assumption 1, we have $\bar{\Delta}_{k}\in[0,1]$ .

We first study arm 1. Since it is the best arm, we hope it is always kept in the active set, and we control the probability of accidental elimination using the definition of Algorithm 3 as following.

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(1\notin\mathcal{A}_{s+1},~1\in\mathcal{A}_{s}\right) \displaystyle~\leq~\mathsf{P}\left(1\in\mathcal{A}_{s},~\exists k\in\mathcal{A}_{s}\setminus\{1\}:~m_{k}^{(s)}-m_{1}^{(s)}>2^{-s}\sigma\right) \displaystyle~\leq~\sum_{k=2}^{K}\mathsf{P}\left(m_{k}^{(s)}-m_{1}^{(s)}>2^{-s}\sigma\right) \displaystyle~\leq~\sum_{k=2}^{K}\mathsf{P}\left(\frac{1}{2\sigma}\left((m_{k}^{(s)}-\bar{\mu}_{k})-(m_{1}^{(s)}-\bar{\mu}_{1})\right)>\frac{1}{2}(\bar{\Delta}_{k}/\sigma+2^{-s})\right) \displaystyle~\leq~K\exp\left(-\frac{n_{s}(\bar{\Delta}_{k}/\sigma+2^{-s})^{2}}{4}\right), $$

where the last inequality is due to the concentration for the mean of $2n_{s}$ independent unit-variance sub-Gaussian random variables. For the event that arm 1 is eliminated, since we choose $n_{s}\geq 2^{2+2s}\log(KTs^{2})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(\exists s:1\notin\mathcal{A}_{s}\right)\leq\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\mathsf{P}\left(1\notin\mathcal{A}_{s+1},1\in\mathcal{A}_{s}\right)\leq K\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\exp\left(-\frac{n_{s}2^{-2s}}{4}\right)\leq K\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{KTs^{2}}~\leq~\frac{2}{T}. $$

Next we study the elimination of a suboptimal arm $k$ . Similarly, we can establish

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(k\in\mathcal{A}_{s+1},~1\in\mathcal{A}_{s},~k\in\mathcal{A}_{s}\right) \displaystyle~\leq~\mathsf{P}\left(1\in\mathcal{A}_{s},~k\in\mathcal{A}_{s},~m_{k}^{(s)}-m_{1}^{(s)}>-2^{-s}\sigma\right) \displaystyle~\leq~\exp\left(-\frac{n_{s}(\bar{\Delta}_{k}/\sigma-2^{-s})^{2}}{4}\right). $$

Define $s_{k}\coloneqq\min\left\{s\geq 1:2^{-s+1}\leq\bar{\Delta}_{k}/\sigma\right\}$ , which is a round highly unlikely to be reached by arm $k$ . For the event that arm $k$ stays in the active set and is not eliminated in round $s_{k}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{P}\left(k\in\mathcal{A}_{s_{k}+1}\right) \displaystyle~\leq~\mathsf{P}\left(k\in\mathcal{A}_{s_{k}+1},1\in\mathcal{A}_{s_{k}},k\in\mathcal{A}_{s_{k}}\right)+\mathsf{P}\left(1\notin\mathcal{A}_{s_{k}}\right) \displaystyle~\leq~\exp\left(-\frac{n_{s_{k}}(\bar{\Delta}_{k}/\sigma-2^{-s_{k}})^{2}}{4}\right)+\frac{2}{T} \displaystyle~\leq~\exp\left(-\frac{n_{s_{k}}2^{-2s_{k}}}{4}\right)+\frac{2}{T} \displaystyle~\leq~\frac{3}{T}. $$

There is also a natural upper bound $\lceil T/(KT_{1})\rceil$ for the number of screening rounds that arm $k$ can survive, because each round takes at least $KT_{1}$ epochs. Here we make a mild assumption that the decision horizon is not too short, so at least one screen round can be completed for all arms, i.e., $T\geq KT_{1}(1+4\log(KT))$ .

Let $C_{k}(T)$ count the total number of epochs that arm $k$ has been pulled. We can derive the following by using (C-51) and $n_{s}\leq 2^{2+2s}\log(KTs^{2})+T_{1}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{E}\left[C_{k}(T)\right] \displaystyle~\leq~T\mathsf{P}\left(k\in\mathcal{A}_{s_{k+1}}\right)~+\sum_{s=1}^{s_{k}\land\lceil T/(KT_{1})\rceil}n_{s} \displaystyle~\leq~3~+\sum_{s=1}^{s_{k}\land\lceil T/(KT_{1})\rceil}2^{2+2s}\log(KTs^{2})+T_{1}s_{k}. $$

If $\bar{\Delta}_{k}\geq\sigma$ , then $s_{k}=1$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{E}\left[C_{k}(T)\right]~\leq~3+4\log(KT)+T_{1}. $$

If $\bar{\Delta}_{k}<\sigma$ , the definition of $s_{k}$ implies $\bar{\Delta}_{k}/\sigma<2^{-s_{k}+2}$ , which leads to $2^{2s_{k}}<16\sigma^{2}/\bar{\Delta}_{k}^{2}$ and $s_{k}<\log_{2}(4\sigma/\bar{\Delta}_{k})$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{E}\left[C_{k}(T)\right] \displaystyle~\leq~3+\log(KT\lceil T/(KT_{1})\rceil^{2})\sum_{s=1}^{s_{k}}2^{2+2s}+T_{1}\log_{2}(4\sigma/\bar{\Delta}_{k}) \displaystyle~\leq~3+\frac{256\sigma^{2}}{3\bar{\Delta}_{k}^{2}}\log(KT^{3})+T_{1}\log_{2}(4\sigma/\bar{\Delta}_{k}), $$

where we bound the geometric series and use a simple fact $\lceil T/(KT_{1})\rceil<T$ in the last step. After combining (C-52) and (C-53), we can bound the expected number of pulls as

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{E}\left[C_{k}(T)\right] \displaystyle~\leq~3+4\log(KT)+\frac{256\sigma^{2}}{3\bar{\Delta}_{k}^{2}}\log(KT^{3})+T_{1}\left(1\lor\log_{2}(4\sigma/\bar{\Delta}_{k})\right). $$

The proof relies on the regret decomposition (Lemma 4.5 in LS2020). Due to the special design of Algorithm 3 that each arm is explored for a certain amount of complete periods, i.e., $n_{s}$ chosen in Step 4 is a multiple of $T_{1}$ , we may utilize the average suboptimal gap over a period to express the total regret incurred by pulling arm $k$ as $\bar{\Delta}_{k}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(T)]$ . There is a trivial issue that the last period of the arm pulled at the end of $T$ may be incomplete if $T$ is not a multiple of $T_{1}$ . It can be simply fixed by extending the decision horizon $T$ to the nearest multiple of $T_{1}$ , namely $\tilde{T}=\lceil T/T_{1}\rceil T_{1}$ , and then we can show

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{E}[R^{\pi}_{T}]\leq\mathsf{E}[R_{\tilde{T}}^{\pi}]=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bar{\Delta}_{k}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(\tilde{T})] \displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bar{\Delta}_{k}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(T)]+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(\tilde{T})-C_{k}(T)], \displaystyle\mathsf{E}[R^{\pi}_{T}] \displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bar{\Delta}_{k}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(T)]+T_{1}. $$

Above inequalities hold because $\bar{\Delta}_{k}\leq 1$ and the total number of epochs added from $T$ to $\tilde{T}$ , i.e., $\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(\tilde{T})-C_{k}(T)]$ , is less than $T_{1}$ .

Finally, we bound the regret by plugging (C-54) into (C-55) as

$$ \begin{split}\mathsf{E}[R^{\pi}_{T}]~\leq~&\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bar{\Delta}_{k}\left(3+4\log(KT)\right)}_{\text{1st term}}~+~\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\frac{256\sigma^{2}}{3\bar{\Delta}_{k}}\log(KT^{3})\right)\land\left(\bar{\Delta}_{k}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(T)]\right)}_{\text{2nd term}}\\
&~+~\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bar{\Delta}_{k}\left(T_{1}\left(1\lor\log_{2}(4\sigma/\bar{\Delta}_{k})\right)\right)+T_{1}}_{\text{3rd term}}.\end{split} $$

For terms in (C-56), we have

$$ \displaystyle\leq\left(3+4\log(KT)\right)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bar{\Delta}_{k}\leq\left(3+4\log(KT)\right)K, \displaystyle\leq\frac{16\sigma}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{\log(KT^{3})}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(T)]}\leq\frac{16\sigma}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{\log(KT^{3})}\sqrt{TK}, \displaystyle\leq T_{1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\bar{\Delta}_{k}\lor 4\sigma\right)+T_{1}\leq T_{1}K(1+4\sigma)+T_{1}. $$

When deriving (C-58), we use the following facts, $\min\{a/\bar{\Delta}_{k},b\bar{\Delta}_{k}\}\leq\sqrt{ab}$ for $a,b\geq 0$ , Jensen’s inequality $\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(T)]}\leq\sqrt{K\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(T)]}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathsf{E}[C_{k}(T)]=T$ .

The 1st term in (C-57) and the 2nd term in (C-58) are $\tilde{O}{(\sqrt{TK})}$ . The 3rd term in (C-59) is also $\tilde{O}{(\sqrt{TK})}$ if $T_{1}\leq\sqrt{T/K}$ , which is actually a milder requirement than Assumption 3. Therefore, we conclude that Algorithm 3 attains a regret upper bound $\tilde{O}{(\sqrt{TK})}$ . ∎
